question: Two swimmers start from the same point on a riverbank. The river flows at \(3\ \text{m/s}\). Swimmer A swims perpendicular to the bank at \(4\ \text{m/s}\) relative to water; Swimmer B aims to reach the point directly opposite A's starting point. If the river is \(120\ \text{m}\) wide, find the ratio of times taken by A and B to cross.
solution: A drifts downstream while crossing: crossing time \(t_A=\dfrac{120}{4}=30\,\text{s}\) (drift doesn't affect crossing time). B must angle upstream so the resultant is straight across: needs \(v_B\sin\theta=3\), so B's effective crossing speed is \(\sqrt{v_B^2-9}\); with \(v_B=4\), that is \(\sqrt7\), giving \(t_B=\dfrac{120}{\sqrt7}\approx45.4\,\text{s}\).\[\dfrac{t_A}{t_B}=\dfrac{\sqrt7}{4}\approx0.66\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: “Crossing time” only ever depends on the perpendicular velocity component — the current changes where you land, never how long it takes, unless you're forced to cancel the drift.

question: A block on a frictionless incline of angle \(\theta\) is connected over a pulley at the top to a hanging mass. Using the fact that the string is inextensible, relate the block's acceleration along the incline to the hanging mass's vertical acceleration.
solution: Let \(x\) be the block's distance from the pulley along the incline and \(y\) the hanging mass's distance below the pulley. String length \(x+y=\text{const}\Rightarrow \dot x+\dot y=0\Rightarrow \ddot x=-\ddot y\).\[|a_{\text{block along incline}}|=|a_{\text{hanging mass}}|\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Write the string-length constraint as an equation first, then differentiate twice — never assume equal accelerations “by symmetry” for an unfamiliar pulley layout.

question: A particle is projected with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) on level ground. Show that the horizontal range formula \(R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}\) gives the same range for \(\theta\) and \(90^\circ-\theta\), and check the \(\theta\to0\) limit makes physical sense.
solution: \(\sin(2(90^\circ-\theta))=\sin(180^\circ-2\theta)=\sin2\theta\), so the range is identical — confirms complementary angles share a range. As \(\theta\to0\), \(\sin2\theta\to0\Rightarrow R\to0\): a horizontal launch along the ground travels zero range before “landing,” which matches intuition.
answer: Range symmetric about 45°; R → 0 as θ → 0, as expected
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Whenever a formula has a free parameter, test \(\theta\to0\) or \(\theta\to90^\circ\) — a wrong derivation almost always breaks at one of the extremes.
